Day 1
From Hotel: 14 min · 5 min → Dallas Museum of Art
1. Dallas Museum of Art
The Dallas Museum of Art spans 24,000 years of world art across 24 galleries with strength in pre-Columbian, South Asian, and American art. The permanent collection is free and open to the public.

2. Nasher Sculpture Center
The Nasher Sculpture Center holds one of the world's premier private sculpture collections in a Renzo Piano–designed building and garden. Works by Rodin, Picasso, Matisse, Giacometti, and Serra fill the naturally lit galleries and garden pavilions.

3. Klyde Warren Park
Klyde Warren Park is a 5.2-acre public park built on a concrete deck over the Woodall Rodgers Freeway, connecting downtown Dallas to Uptown. The great lawn, children's garden, dog park, and food trucks anchor civic life at the foot of the Arts District.

4. Perot Museum of Nature and Science
The Perot Museum is a Morphosis-designed natural history and science museum with 11 permanent halls covering paleontology, geology, space, and engineering. The building's dramatic tilted-cube form is a Dallas architectural landmark.

5. Dallas World Aquarium
The Dallas World Aquarium occupies a converted 1913 warehouse with a five-story tropical rainforest atrium housing over 85,000 specimens. Manatees, orinoco crocodiles, jaguars, arapaima, and hundreds of free-flying tropical birds inhabit interconnected environments across multiple levels.

Day 2
From Hotel: 15 min → Hall of State
1. Hall of State
The Hall of State is the signature building of the 1936 Texas Centennial Exposition at Fair Park — an Art Deco masterpiece with a gilded Great Hall, bronze entry doors, and WPA murals documenting Texas history. It is a National Historic Landmark and the finest Art Deco building in the state.
Read more

2. African American Museum
The African American Museum, Dallas holds one of the largest African American fine art collections in the southern United States, spread across four wings of folk art, religious art, and contemporary works documenting African American experience and cultural heritage from enslavement through the civil rights era.

3. Reunion Tower Geo-Deck
The Reunion Tower Geo-Deck is a 470-foot outdoor observation platform on Dallas's most recognizable landmark — a geodesic sphere atop a 561-foot tower — with 360-degree panoramic views of the skyline, high-definition telescopes, and interactive touchscreens identifying landmarks across the horizon.

1. Dallas Arboretum and Botanical Garden
The Dallas Arboretum covers 66 acres along the eastern shore of White Rock Lake, with 19 themed gardens including the eight-acre Lay Family Garden. The grounds are known for seasonal floral displays — tulips in spring, dahlias in fall — and sweeping views across the lake from the garden terraces.

1. The Sixth Floor Museum
The Sixth Floor Museum occupies the former Texas School Book Depository floor used in the Kennedy assassination of November 1963. Exhibits document the assassination, investigation, and Kennedy's presidency, with the sniper's perch preserved behind glass.

2. Pioneer Plaza
Pioneer Plaza holds the world's largest bronze sculpture — 49 life-size longhorn cattle and 3 trail-riding cowboys across 4.2 landscaped acres with a waterfall. Sculptor Robert Summers made every steer at six feet high, commemorating the historic Shawnee Trail cattle drives.

3. George W. Bush Presidential Library and Museum
The George W. Bush Presidential Library covers Bush's presidency through the Decision Points Theater, where visitors confront intelligence and options behind decisions on 9/11, Hurricane Katrina, and the 2008 financial crisis. A replica Oval Office and Freedom Garden complete the SMU campus.

4. Meadows Museum
The Meadows Museum holds one of the most comprehensive collections of Spanish art outside Spain — 900 objects from the 10th to 21st century. Algur Meadows built a Prado of the Americas on the SMU campus; works by Velázquez, Goya, Picasso, Miró, and Dalí span painting, sculpture, and works on paper.

5. Crow Museum of Asian Art
The Crow Museum of Asian Art holds 1,500 objects from South Asia, Southeast Asia, China, Japan, and Korea spanning antiquity to the 20th century. Assembled by Trammell Crow from the 1960s, the free Arts District museum opened in 1998. Highlights include a Chola Shiva Nataraja bronze, Song dynasty ceramics, and jade.

1. Kimbell Art Museum
The Kimbell Art Museum is widely considered the finest small art museum in the United States: roughly 350 works from antiquity to the early 20th century, housed in Louis Kahn's 1972 cycloid concrete vaults, each split by a narrow skylight. Highlights include Fra Angelico, Caravaggio's The Cardsharps, and Rembrandt.
Read more

2. Amon Carter Museum of American Art
The Amon Carter Museum holds the largest Frederic Remington collection in existence alongside Charles Russell, Thomas Eakins's The Swimming Hole, Winslow Homer, Georgia O'Keeffe, and a premier photography archive including Ansel Adams. Philip Johnson's 1961 limestone building is adjacent to the Kimbell.
Read more

12 min → Fort Worth Stockyards
3. Fort Worth Stockyards
The Fort Worth Stockyards preserves the 98-acre former livestock market that made this one of the five largest meatpacking centers in the country by the 1940s. Longhorn cattle are driven down Exchange Avenue daily — 11:30am and 4:00pm — the world's only remaining authentic cattle drive. Entry is free.

Local Tastes
Texas Barbecue
Dallas-style barbecue features oak-smoked brisket sliced from the flat and the point, pork ribs, and jalapeño-cheddar sausage served on butcher paper with white bread and pickles.
Pecan Lodge · Deep Ellum
Tex-Mex
Dallas Tex-Mex traces a direct line from border cantinas — enchiladas smothered in chili gravy, puffy tacos, and frozen margaritas that the city claims to have invented.
El Fenix · Uptown
Fletcher's Corny Dog
The State Fair of Texas invented the corny dog — a hot dog on a stick dipped in cornmeal batter and deep-fried — and Fletcher's has made them at Fair Park since the fair's earliest decades.
Fair Park
Frozen Margarita
Dallas lays claim to the world's first frozen margarita machine, installed at Mariano Martinez's restaurant in 1971 — the original machine is now in the Smithsonian.
Mariano's
Food Delivery
DoorDash
Foreign number: accepted.
The dominant delivery platform in Dallas with the widest restaurant selection across Uptown, Deep Ellum, and the Design District; excellent coverage of local Tex-Mex, barbecue, and burger spots alongside national chains; generally reliable on timing in the dense inner neighborhoods.
doordash.com
Uber Eats
Foreign number: accepted.
Strong Dallas presence particularly in Uptown and around the Arts District; useful for visitors who already have an Uber account since the experience is identical; good restaurant variety including a number of spots not listed on DoorDash.
ubereats.com
Grubhub
Foreign number: not accepted. — a US mobile number is required to sign up.
Solid backup option in Dallas with good coverage of the central and Uptown districts; occasionally lists local and independent restaurants not found on the other platforms; worth checking if the other apps show limited options in your area.

Getting Around
Uber
Foreign number: accepted.
The most widely used ride-hailing option in Dallas with strong supply across Uptown, the Arts District, Deep Ellum, and out to the Bishop Arts District; reliable for late-night returns and runs to the convention center; surge pricing applies during Cowboys, Stars, and Mavericks game nights.
uber.com
Lyft
Foreign number: accepted.

Worth Knowing

A Glass Tower's Glare Waged War on a Sculpture Garden

When the 42-story Museum Tower opened next to the Nasher Sculpture Center in 2011, its curved glass facade reflected concentrated sunlight directly onto the museum's Renzo Piano–designed garden and gallery roof. The heat scorched plantings, forced curators to move works — including a Picasso — indoors to protect them, and knocked out a site-specific James Turrell skyspace, whose open view of the sky the tower now permanently intruded on. A mediator brought in to broker a fix resigned after both sides rejected every proposed remedy, from tinting the tower's windows to erecting a 400-foot freestanding shade structure, and the dispute quietly ended with no resolution at all — the glare is simply still there.

Klyde Warren Park carries the name of a boy who was nine years old when it opened. Pipeline executive Kelcy Warren made a lead gift toward building the deck park over Woodall Rodgers Freeway and used the naming rights not for himself but for his young son. The arrangement came with one unusual condition: as part of the naming agreement, Klyde himself is obligated to help pick up litter in the park once a month — possibly the only namesake in the country contractually bound to clean his own park.
